ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening against the UN Consolidated List, all Canadian sanctions regulations promulgated under the Special Economic Measures Act (Canada) and the United Nations Act (including restrictions applying to Russia, Iran, Syria and Venezuela), the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list required for USD clearing through Visa/Mastercard networks and Fedwire, and domestic FINTRAC suspicious transaction reporting triggers. The PSP must implement a PCMLTFA s. 9.6 compliance program with mandatory identification and enhanced due diligence of all politically exposed persons (PEPs) and heads of international organizations as defined in the PCMLTFA, including determination of PEP status of every beneficial owner, source of wealth and source of funds verification, ongoing transaction monitoring, and merchant-level sub-SDN screening for all cross-border counterparties.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (REQ) online service portal, Registre des entreprises du Québec; federal alternative: Corporations Canada Online Filing Centre (NUANS-based incorporation system)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Charter of the French Language (C.Q.L.R. c. C-11), a Quebec provincial corporate name must be in French; bilingual names are permissible only where a French version is registered, and the French version must be used in public signs, invoices and legal documentation in Quebec. Names in non-Latin scripts must be transliterated into the Latin alphabet; the name must be distinctive, must not be confusingly similar to any existing enterprise in the REQ register, and must not falsely suggest government affiliation, regulated lending, or provision of professional services subject to reserved title. For a federal CBCA corporation with a Quebec registered office, a French or bilingual name is mandatory for the first corporate name.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: bank / banque (requires prior federal authorization under the Bank Act)
insurance / assurance (requires licensing under Quebec and federal insurance statutes)
loan / prêt or finance / financement (restricted as implying regulated financial services without licence)
securities / valeurs mobilières (restricted without applicable dealer or marketplace authorization)
university / université and college / collège (restricted educational terms)
engineer / ingénieur (professional title protected by Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec)
architect / architecte (professional title protected by Ordre des architectes du Québec)
Canada / gouvernement du Canada (connotes Crown affiliation; requires ministerial consent)
Royal / Royale and Crown / Couronne (restricted monarchic and Crown tokens)
Québec (territorial denomination may be used only descriptively without misleading connotation)
Incorporated / Inc. or Corporation / Corp. (legal form suffixes permitted only after actual articles of incorporation are filed)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon REQ refusal of a reserved name, the applicant may submit a fresh name reservation request with a revised name, or contest the registrar's decision by way of an application to the Court of Québec under ss. 42-44 of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises; a rejected name may also be examined for confusion against the existing register before re-filing. For the federal route, a name rejected by Corporations Canada may be remedied by filing further written representations to the Director of Corporate Registries and, if necessary, by an application for judicial review to the Federal Court under s. 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, or simply by a new NUANS search with a different name within the 90-day reservation window.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual-office or registered-agent arrangement is permissible only where it provides a genuine physical street address in Quebec, a professional agent for service of process, and forwarding of legal and regulatory correspondence; P.O. boxes and mail-only drops are statutorily prohibited as the registered office. For a cross-border payment gateway classified as a money services business, FINTRAC additionally requires a physical place of business in Canada where books, records and the AML/CFT compliance program are kept, so a virtual office without operational staff or local records does not constitute sufficient commercial substance for MSB licensing and card-network registration purposes.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: High: estimated 65-85% probability of an announced or unannounced physical on-site inspection by FINTRAC, Revenu Québec or the Autorité des marchés financiers within the first 24 months of operation for a high-risk cross-border PSP, with additional escalation risk from Visa/Mastercard member-registration compliance audits.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act, CQLR c S-31.1, as amended; ss. 9, 10, 14, 16–22 (incorporation and articles), 46–49 (registered office and corporate records), 51–58 (directors), 62–64 (officers), 66–71 (share subscriptions and issue), 78–82 (shareholder meetings), 101, 112–113 (amendments and by-laws), 124–126 (financial statements), 169–171 (dissolution).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registraire des entreprises (Québec Business Registry), a directorate of Investissement Québec, operating under the Ministry of the Economy, Innovation and Energy; online portal at reg.entreprises.gouv.qc.ca.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of incorporation (statuts de constitution) filed electronically through the Registraire des entreprises under section 10 of the Québec Business Corporations Act; the issued certificate is the certificate of incorporation.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital exists under the QBCA; a corporation may be incorporated with zero issued shares. The articles must specify an authorized share capital, commonly an unlimited number of common shares. There is no escrow-account requirement for ordinary incorporation; escrowed funds may arise only in private placements under securities laws if public capital is raised.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that the incorporator(s) hereby subscribe for the initial common shares set out in the subscription schedule, that the subscription be accepted, and that the shares be allotted and issued as fully paid upon receipt of the stated consideration. RESOLVED that the registered office of the Corporation be and is hereby established at the address set out in the accompanying notice, and that the Corporate Secretary forthwith file the notice with the Registraire des entreprises. RESOLVED that the persons named in the officer appointment schedule be and are hereby appointed President, Secretary, and Treasurer, respectively, each with the usual powers of such office, effective immediately. CERTIFIED by the Chair of the first board meeting this ___ day of ___, 20___.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate name reservation and distinctness clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises – online name-reservation service at reg.entreprises.gouv.qc.ca
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a prior search in the Québec enterprise register to determine whether the proposed name is distinct and complies with the QBCA naming rules. Submit an optional name-reservation request; if no reservation is made, the name will be examined as part of the articles filing. Ensure the name includes a legal element such as 'Corporation', 'Inc.', 'Ltée' or an approved abbreviation.
required_dossiers: Proposed corporate name in French, with an English version if desired
Brief description of the corporation's principal business activity
Name-analysis request form (where applicable)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registrar refuses the name, file a new naming request or an amended reservation within 30 days; administrative correction and re-submission are permitted without court intervention except where trademark infringement is alleged.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and execution of the articles of incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Incorporator(s) and corporate counsel; no government filing at this stage
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the articles of incorporation in French or English using the registrar's model bylaws or an approved precedent. Insert the corporation's name, registered office address, share structure, director count, any restriction on share transfers, and limitations on the corporation's business. Each incorporator must sign the final draft and date it before submission.
required_dossiers: Completed draft articles of incorporation
Name-reservation certificate (if obtained)
Consent of each incorporator to act as such
Proposed registered office address within Québec
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registrar queries a clause, amend the draft and re-execute; the corporation may also proceed with a corrected filing if the original has not yet been processed.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Statutory filing of articles and issuance of certificate of incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the executed articles electronically through the Registraire des entreprises' 'Déclaration d'immatriculation' portal. Pay the applicable filing fee online, verify the attached enterprise registration information, and await the certificate of incorporation. The certificate is effective on the date shown in the certificate or, if no later date is stated, on the date the registrar receives the completed application.
required_dossiers: Executed articles of incorporation
Proof of payment of the statutory filing fee
Notice of registered office address (if not included in the articles)
Statement of the intended principal activity
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is rejected or formally queried, the applicant may file corrected articles within the registrar's prescribed period and pay any amended fee; procedural refusals may be appealed to the Court of Québec under the QBCA.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First board meeting, organizational by-laws, share issuance and officer appointments
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of directors of the newly incorporated corporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold the first meeting of directors after incorporation. Adopt organizational by-laws, confirm the registered office address, approve the issuance of the common shares to the incorporators, and appoint the President, Secretary, Treasurer, and any other required officers. Record the decisions in formal minutes signed by the chair and the secretary. If the registered office address differs from that in the articles, file the change electronically with the Registraire des entreprises.
required_dossiers: Notice of registered office (if changed after filing)
First board meeting minutes
Organizational by-laws
Resolution approving share subscription and allotment
Resolution appointing officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the notice of registered office is rejected, correct the address formatting and re-file; the effective date of the correction will be the date of the successful re-filing, and the directors should ratify actions taken in the interim.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises; Revenu Québec; Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); FINTRAC; Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Within 30 days of the certificate of incorporation, obtain a federal business number from the CRA, register for GST/HST and QST with Revenu Québec, register for employer payroll deductions if the corporation will hire personnel, and submit the Quebec enterprise registration update. Concurrently, as a payment-service provider, register as a money-services business with FINTRAC and apply to the AMF for authorization under Quebec's Money-Services Businesses Act before commencing regulated activities.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation
Quebec enterprise registration certificate (attestation)
CRA and Revenu Québec tax registrations
Corporate criminal background and identity records for officers
Anti-money laundering compliance program and designated compliance officer
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Failure to register is a continuing offence; cure by immediately filing the overdue federal and provincial registrations, paying any applicable penalties, and submitting a written explanation. The AMF may act by warning, suspension, or licence revocation; an appeal lies to the Financial and Administrative Tribunal of Québec.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF), coordinated with FINTRAC (Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada) for anti-money-laundering oversight; municipal and provincial building-safety authorities for physical workplaces.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Money-Services Business (MSB) registration under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17), and a money-services business licence issued by the AMF under the Act respecting money-services businesses (CQLR c S-5).

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP)
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt – the principal activity is digital payment processing and clearing, which does not constitute an industrial activity listed under the Environment Quality Act (CQLR c Q-2); the corporation may request an attestation of non-application for the proposed office use.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable for a data-only office environment. If auxiliary data-centre equipment with standby diesel generators is installed, generator emissions must meet the thresholds of the Clean Air Act (CQLR c Q-2) and the Regulation respecting the application of the Environment Quality Act; electronic waste must be managed under Éco-PAC and municipal e-waste disposal bylaws.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification for the registered office and operating premises under the Quebec Fire Safety Code, including a fire-prevention plan and annual verification; structural load and occupancy clearance issued by the municipal building inspector for the leased or owned office; registration with the CNESST under the Act respecting occupational health and safety (CQLR c S-2.1) and posting of the occupational health and safety policy, first-aid kit and emergency evacuation plan.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency / Agence du revenu du Canada (CRA) for federal GST/HST, Part I and Part XIV corporate income tax, payroll, and excise; Revenu Québec (RQ) for Quebec Sales Tax (QST), provincial corporate income tax, and Quebec employer contributions. Portals: CRA My Business Account and Business Registration Online (canada.ca/en/revenue-agency); Revenu Québec Cl@SSE portal (www.revenuquebec.ca).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign-incorporated payment-service provider carrying on business in Canada obtains a CRA Business Number (BN) via Business Registration Online or Form RC1, quoting its foreign certificate of incorporation and appointing a Canadian attorney for service; program accounts RC (Part I/Part XIV income tax), RT (GST/HST), RP (payroll) and RM (import-export) are activated under the same BN. For Quebec, the entity must first obtain a Quebec Enterprise Number (NEQ) from the Registraire des entreprises du Québec, which single-window enrollment then opens the Revenu Québec QST account (NR prefix), the provincial income-tax account and employer accounts. CRA and RQ exchange registration data, but the taxpayer must separately declare its financial-institution status for QST attribution. Where the gateway is non-resident, simplified non-resident GST/HST registration applies and the federal branch is exposed to Part XIV branch tax on Canadian-source operating income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation: a Business Corporation is a separate taxpayer resident in Canada taxed under ITA Part I on worldwide income; for non-resident corporations the scope is source-based taxation plus Part XIV 25% branch tax. No check-the-box or pass-through eligibility applies; no tax-exempt-zone status applies to a commercial PSP in Quebec. Federal general corporate rate is 15% (28% base less 13% general reduction), with the CCPC small-business rate at 9% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income; Quebec adds provincial rates of 11.5% general and 5% for qualified small-business income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No US check-the-box election exists; entity-level taxation is automatic. Relevant statutory elections include: ETA s.156 joint election of closely related registrants to treat intercompany supplies as taxable; ETA s.150(1) GST25 election by a financial institution to treat otherwise-exempt financial services as taxable so the PSP can claim input tax credits on acquiring, gateway and interchange infrastructure; ITA s.85 rollover election to transfer merchant contracts and software IP into the Canadian corporation on a tax-deferred basis; ITA s.93(2) and s.113 elections for foreign-affiliate surplus repatriation; CCPC classification and associated-corporation elections under ITA ss.125 and 256; and the 2024 interest-limitation (EIFEL) election, waiver and filing mechanics set by ITA ss.18.2 to 18.21, with transfer-pricing documentation under ITA s.247(4).

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Canada GST/HST plus Quebec Sales Tax (QST) administered as a dual-but-harmonized indirect-tax regime; Quebec is a non-HST province, so the domestic headline is 5% federal GST plus 9.975% QST. Payment clearing, merchant acquiring, authorization and settlement services of a PSP are exempt financial supplies under ETA Schedule V, Part VII; export-oriented financial services to foreign merchants are zero-rated under ETA Schedule VI, Part II s.20 and Schedule VI, Part V s.7. A separate 3% federal Digital Services Tax (S.C. 2024, c.12) applies from 2024 to qualifying online-intermediation groups, with acquirer fees potentially in scope.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000: GST/HST small-supplier threshold (ETA s.148) and the identical QST registration threshold; taxable supplies of goods and services made worldwide determine the threshold, while zero-rated export supplies and settlement flows are excluded; voluntary registration is available below CAD 30,000 to recover input tax credits.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control or digital stamping exists at any Canadian level. Canada operates the voluntary Pan-Canadian E-Invoicing Service (PCEI) on Peppol BIS 3.0 for B2B and B2G; CRA and Revenu Québec require electronic filing of GST/HST/QST returns by registrants with annual taxable supplies above CAD 1,500,000 and demand that all e-books and records be kept in original machine-readable form for six years. For a PSP, daily interchange clearing records, merchant settlement balance files and Fedwire/Visa/Mastercard network trace data constitute the primary fiscal evidence trail.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods exported from Canada are zero-rated under ETA Schedule VI, Part V ss.16-17 with proof of export (supplier export or delivery to a carrier). Services, including acquiring and clearing services, are zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V s.7 when supplied to a non-resident who is not registered and does not use the service in a Canadian business or in relation to Canadian real or capital property; financial services supplied to non-resident non-registrants are zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part II s.20. For the cross-border payment gateway, fees invoiced to foreign merchants on Visa/Mastercard/Fedwire rails qualify only where KYC files evidence foreign residence, settlement is made in foreign currency to a foreign account, and the service is not connected to a Canadian location or Canadian customer base.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canadian Automated Export Declaration (CAED) or Canada Customs Export Declaration line items
Commercial invoice matched to acquirer settlement and interchange fee reports
Bill of Lading, air waybill or electronic transport document for physical export shipments
Inward Remittance Certificate, SWIFT MT103/202, or foreign exchange conversion proof evidencing settlement within 180 days
Merchant KYC and non-resident status file: tax residency certificate, foreign VAT/GST registration, registered business address and board or regulatory attestations
Visa/Mastercard/Fedwire network clearing records with merchant-level transaction trace and reconciliation statements
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may reassess zero-rated export treatment within four years under ETA s.298 and without time limit where misrepresentation or fraud exists; any clawback carries statutory daily compounded interest, plus the ETA s.285 gross-negligence penalty of 5% of underreported net tax and a minimum monetary penalty per false statement. Non-repatriation beyond the 180-day benchmark exposes the receivable to transfer-pricing recharacterization under ITA s.247 and to deemed-interest or dividend treatment, while Revenu Québec mirrors the exposure under the QST Act and the Tax Administration Act s.59 (50% penalty for deliberate or grossly negligent false declarations). Directors and officers face joint and several liability under ETA s.323 for unremitted GST/HST/QST and criminal prosecution under ETA s.327 for knowing evasion, attracting fines up to the amount evaded and imprisonment up to five years on indictment.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada, acting as monetary authority and, since the Retail Payment Activities Act (Canada), as the retail payments supervision authority. Canada has no central foreign-exchange administration: the Foreign Exchange Control Act was repealed in 1951, and no exchange control approval is required by the Bank of Canada or the Minister of Finance for any cross-border payment, capital injection, or profit remittance. Prudential regulation of banks rests with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI); Payments Canada operates Lynx, the high-value Canadian-dollar real-time gross settlement system, and the ACSS batch clearing system. Anti-money-laundering supervision of money services businesses is conducted by FINTRAC under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA); in Quebec, the Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF) licenses Money-Services Businesses under the Money-Services Businesses Act (Quebec).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible for residents and non-residents. Canada imposes no exchange control restrictions on current-account transfers, capital-account transactions, dividends, interest, royalties, management fees, or loan repayments. A Quebec corporation may maintain foreign-currency bank accounts with Canadian Schedule I banks and may freely pay imports, merchant payouts, and third-party suppliers abroad. Profit remittance is constrained only by tax law: non-resident shareholders are subject to Part XIII withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (Canada) at a 25% statutory rate, generally reduced to 15% (portfolio) or 5% (10% ownership) under an applicable tax treaty; a Canadian branch of a non-resident corporation is subject to Part I tax plus 25% branch tax, subject to treaty reduction. Quebec's Taxation Act contains equivalent rules for Quebec-source distributions. The Investment Canada Act also requires a non-Canadian establishing a new Canadian business or acquiring control of a Canadian business to file an initial notification or, above prescribed review thresholds, a net-benefit application. The Gateway must additionally register under the Retail Payment Activities Act with the Bank of Canada and, if operating in Quebec, hold an AMF money-services business licence.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable. Canada has no statutory timeline for repatriating export proceeds, no mandatory conversion of foreign currency into Canadian dollars, and no surrender requirement for payment-gateway settlement balances. Exporters and payment service providers may retain 100% of foreign-currency receipts in Canadian or offshore foreign-currency accounts. The only relevant duties are FINTRAC reporting obligations: cash or monetary instruments of C$10,000 or more crossing the border must be reported to the Canada Border Services Agency (Form E677); large cash transactions at or above C$10,000 within a 24-hour period require a Large Cash Transaction Report; and FINTRAC Travel Rule data, including originator and beneficiary information, must accompany international wire transfers.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium feasibility with substantial legal constraints. Canada has no equivalent of the European 'EMI' or 'payment institution' passport; an offshore digital EMI cannot clear Canadian-dollar payments through Lynx or provide local settlement accounts on its own. The Quebec gateway must itself be the regulated entity: it must be a Canadian resident for FINTRAC MSB registration, hold an AMF money-services business licence for Quebec operations, and maintain a settlement account with a Schedule I bank or with Payments Canada participant bank. An offshore EMI may be used only as a supplementary technology or correspondent partner, provided it is regulated in its home jurisdiction, is not on any sanctions list, and is onboarded by the Canadian bank through a full correspondent-bank due-diligence process. Because OSFI-regulated banks treat cross-border PSPs as high-risk, the gateway should expect enhanced due diligence and a capital-escrow or segregated-client-funds structure. Direct clearing membership in Lynx is not available to the PSP itself; bank sponsorship is required.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Statutory banking law does not require directors to appear physically, and most Canadian banks permit remote onboarding using video verification and notarized corporate documents. In practice, for a high-risk cross-border PSP in Quebec, banks will require at least one authorized director, officer, or Canadian-resident compliance officer to attend an in-branch interview at the bank's Montreal or Quebec City corporate banking centre, or to provide a certified limited power of attorney in favor of a local signatory. A registered office in Quebec is mandatory under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Quebec Business Corporations Act, FINTRAC requires the MSB to maintain a place of business in Canada, and the AMF requires a Quebec establishment for a money-services business licence. Therefore physical presence for corporate and compliance infrastructure, though not for every shareholder, is effectively indispensable for bank onboarding. Non-resident directors may be verified remotely through notarized passport copies, bank references, and apostilled certificates; however the bank will likely require the Chief Compliance Officer to be a Canadian resident.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Newly incorporated Quebec holding or payment company with no audited financial history and with non-Canadian ultimate beneficial owners proposing cross-border merchant settlement.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certificate of incorporation and articles of amendment; Registraire des entreprises attestation; complete UBO chart with identification and residential addresses; source-of-funds and source-of-wealth statements for all principal shareholders; notarized share subscription and capitalization evidence; forecast settlement volumes; corporate business plan; FINTRAC MSB registration certificate; AMF money-services business licence or application receipt; AML/ATF program prepared under the PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance; sanctions screening logs; transaction monitoring policy; appointment of a Canadian-resident compliance officer; ISO/IEC 27001 certificate; PCI DSS Report on Compliance; and evidence of an independent AML audit.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Aggregated sub-merchant payment flows in high-risk MCC codes, including digital wallets, gaming, trading platforms, or crypto-adjacent businesses.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Merchant KYC/KYB files for each sub-merchant; merchant acceptance policy with whitelisted MCC codes; geographic risk matrix; sub-merchant due-diligence questionnaire; segregated trust or escrow account for customer funds; reconciliation and chargeback monitoring procedures; automated transaction monitoring with threshold alerts; Travel Rule data capture for wire transfers; FINTRAC large-cash and suspicious-transaction reporting procedures; internal audit reports; and contractual prohibition of unregistered virtual-asset service providers.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large inbound capital injection from a related foreign entity not clearly matching the corporation's stated share capital or commercial value.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed share subscription agreement; capital call notice; board resolution authorizing issuance; updated share register and securities register; bank statements showing the exact remitting entity, date, amount, and reference; explanation of commercial purpose; valuation report if non-cash consideration is used; Part XIII tax analysis for any deemed benefit; source-of-funds legal opinion from the remitting bank; Investment Canada Act initial notification or review application as applicable; and Quebec business registration amendments reflecting any new shareholders.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border remittances from or to jurisdictions subject to OFAC, Canadian sanctions, FATF monitoring, or high financial-crime risk, or involving money transmitters without a corresponding Canadian registration.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Risk-based country and jurisdiction matrix; OFAC and Canadian Consolidated Autonomous Sanctions List screening policy; real-time screening of counterparties, UBOs, and intermediary banks; wire originator and beneficiary data quality controls; prohibition on processing payments for unlicensed or unregistered money transmitters; contractual list of prohibited counterparties; FINTRAC STR policy; sanctions-free compliance certification from counterparty banking institutions; and independent certification of sanctions screening technology.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Route all inbound equity contributions by SWIFT MT103 in CAD or USD to the corporation's escrow or operational account at the Canadian bank. Canada has no official purpose-code regime and no exchange-control approval; however the bank will require the payment narrative to be transparent, for example 'CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION - SHARE SUBSCRIPTION', together with the corporate enterprise number and the subscribing entity's legal name. The complete verification bundle consists of the share subscription/capital call, board resolution, register of directors and shareholders, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth evidence from the subscriber, and the Canadian bank's standard KYC declaration confirming the ultimate beneficial owners. If the subscriber is a non-Canadian, an Investment Canada Act initial notification must be filed within 30 days; a net-benefit application may be required for an acquisition of control of an existing Canadian business above the applicable review threshold. Physically transported currency or monetary instruments of C$10,000 or more require a CBSA cross-border currency report. The funds become unrestricted working capital once recorded in the accounting system and supported by a dated director resolution.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Use SWIFT MT103 for international trade settlements and merchant payouts to non-Canadian beneficiaries; use MT202 COV for bank-to-bank cover payments. For final Canadian-dollar payments inside Canada, clear through Lynx for real-time high-value transactions and through ACSS for batch merchant payouts, payroll, and pre-authorized debits. For United States-dollar disbursements, clear through Fedwire or CHIPS via the Canadian bank's correspondent network. Commercial letters of credit may be issued or confirmed by the Canadian bank under ICC UCP 600 with reimbursement by MT103 or MT202. Visa and Mastercard acquiring settlement is delivered as net settlement to the gateway's operational account via the card network's daily funding cycle. All outbound wires must transport complete originator and beneficiary data, including legal name, account number, address, and bank identifier, to satisfy the FINTRAC Travel Rule. The Gateway should maintain segregated client-fund or escrow accounts for merchant principal amounts, separate from its own operating funds, while outsourcing final settlement to regulated clearing infrastructure.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright deliverable FX forwards in CAD pairs (CAD/USD, CAD/EUR, CAD/GBP, CAD/JPY) with Canadian Schedule I banks
FX swaps combining a spot leg with a forward leg for short-duration liquidity management
Cross-currency swaps (CAD against USD, EUR, GBP) for long-term hedging of intercompany loans and capital structures
Vanilla over-the-counter FX options and zero-cost collars for contingent merchant payout exposures
Listed CAD/USD futures and options on CME and CI-X for exchange-traded hedging transparency
Non-deliverable CAD forwards (offshore NDFs) usable where physical CAD delivery is impractical; permitted, but generally unnecessary because CAD is a freely convertible, deliverable currency

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA) - online filing with Corporations Canada; applicable only if the company is incorporated federally. A provincial company incorporated under the Quebec Business Corporations Act (QBCA) is not subject to this filing.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary date of incorporation each year (e.g., incorporated on 15 March, due on or before 14 May).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: CAD 50 late-filing penalty in addition to the CAD 12 base fee; failure to file for two or more consecutive years permits the Director to initiate administrative dissolution under CBCA s. 240 after a formal notice and a 120-day cure period.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Declaration (declaration annuelle) under the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, chapter P-44.1.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Last day of the month following the month containing the anniversary of the enterprise's registration (e.g., registered on 15 March, due by 30 April annually).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing triggers a late-fee surcharge and administrative fines of CAD 200-CAD 5,000 for legal persons; administrative strike-off from the REQ register may be initiated after a default of three consecutive years, after which the struck-off enterprise cannot obtain REQ attestation certificates or contract with Quebec public bodies.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual corporation income tax returns: federal T2 and Quebec CO-17, including financial statements and reconciliation schedules.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Revenu Quebec
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end (e.g., 31 December year-end, due by 30 June); balance-due tax payments generally fall due within two or three months after year-end depending on Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) status.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty equal to 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per complete month of delay up to a 12-month maximum, doubled to 10% if a gross-negligence penalty was assessed in the preceding three years, plus prescribed-rate interest; Revenu Quebec imposes parallel sanctions on the CO-17; willful evasion is a criminal offence.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Under QBCA ss. 236-239 and CBCA ss. 155 and 163, an auditor must be appointed at each annual meeting; a non-reporting issuer may dispense with the audit only by unanimous shareholders' resolution renewed annually, and no revenue, asset, or employee-size safe harbor exists in Quebec. Reporting issuers (public companies) are never exempt. The payment gateway's acquirer and card-scheme contracts additionally mandate an annual independent examination (SOC 1/SOC 2 or PCI DSS Level 1 Report on Compliance) as a commercial scheme-rule requirement.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian GAAP per the CPA Canada Handbook - IFRS for reporting issuers; Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE, Part II) available to private corporations. The chosen framework must be applied consistently and reconciled to CRA and Revenu Quebec tax schedules (T2/CO-17).

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Under CBCA s. 21.1 (federal companies), the corporation must maintain an internal Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) register identifying any holder of 25% or more of voting shares or a controlling influence; share transfers that change ISC rights must be recorded in the ISC register and the share transfer ledger within 15 days. The CBCA annual return requires confirmation that the ISC register has been maintained and is available for inspection. For Quebec-incorporated (QBCA) companies, no ISC-style filing is made with the REQ; the annual declaration confirms the registered office, directors, and officers, while any share transfer is recorded in the Register of Members. Full UBO schedules are filed publicly only where the corporation is a reporting issuer or qualifies as a 'public enterprise' or 'large enterprise' holding government contracts under Quebec's Act respecting transparency in public contracts.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (minutes of shareholders' and board meetings and resolutions)
Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) register - mandatory for CBCA-incorporated corporations (CBCA s. 21.1)
Share transfer ledger / central securities register

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 250-650 per year (CAD 350-900) for registered office and corporate agent services in Quebec, as quoted by Montreal-area law firms and national corporate service providers.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 12,000-35,000 per year (CAD 16,000-45,000) for an independent audit of a private cross-border payment gateway, including coordination of SOC 1/SOC 2 and PCI DSS Level 1 reporting; a review engagement may cost USD 4,000-9,000 per year where the audit is waived by unanimous shareholder resolution.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.2% combined Quebec and federal headline rate for a Quebec active business corporation (11.5% federal general rate plus 11.5% Quebec provincial rate, before the federal general rate reduction and provincial abatement mechanics; actual combined effective statutory rate on active business income is approximately 26.2% in Quebec for 2025, assuming no M&P reduction and standard rate settings)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction (SBD) reduces the federal rate to 9% on active business income up to CAD 500,000, which combined with Quebec's reduced 5% small business rate yields an approximate 12.2% combined rate on eligible small business income within the business limit, subject to international income allocation and corporate group business limit sharing rules; accelerated capital cost allowance for eligible digital assets and software, scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) investment tax credits of up to 15% (federal) plus Quebec's 14% refundable R&D tax credit, and the Quebec refundable tax credit for e-business and payment technology innovation in certain qualifying conditions; intercorporate dividend deductions on dividends received from Canadian resident corporations; treaty-based foreign tax credits on cross-border income to reduce double taxation.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed via the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) GST/HST NETFILE, E-FILE, or the CRA My Business Account portal, accompanied by Quebec Revenu Quebec form CO-17 (Société – Déclaration de revenus) filed via Revenu Quebec's Corporation Internet Transmit service (ED@S), plus schedule CO-1108 (Federal rules reconciliation) and supporting Quebec schedules; Schedule 1 (Federal active business income allocation), Schedule 3 (Provincial territorial corporation income allocation), Schedule 91 (Quebec designated corporation and foreign affiliate information), and applicable T2 schedules for capital gains, investment tax credits, and Part I tax.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Corporations with a taxation year-end must file the T2 return no later than six months after the end of the taxation year (Section 150 of the Income Tax Act (Canada)); Quebec CO-17 generally due no later than six months after fiscal year-end; quarterly corporate income tax installment payments are required for corporations with federal taxable income exceeding thresholds (typically taxes payable above CAD 3,000), based on estimated prior-year or current-year tax, and Revenu Quebec has comparable quarterly installment requirements for Quebec corporate income tax.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 page 1, Box 250 (Revenu Quebec CO-17, Box 175)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Fiscal year-end, legal name, business number (BN), Canada Revenue Agency program account (RC0001), Quebec enterprise registrar (NEQ) if applicable, incorporation jurisdiction, and provincial allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident foreign corporations carrying on business in Canada or disposing of taxable Canadian property must indicate non-resident status, the permanent establishment in Quebec, and the treaty article number (Canada–Quebec internal allocation is not treaty-based; use Canada Tax Treaty article and Form T2/NR or T2 Schedule 91 to report Canadian branch operations).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 1, Line 400 (Revenu Quebec CO-17, Box 125)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income including worldwide business income, property income, capital gains, and international cross-border transaction fees from merchant discount and interchange fees.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident PSP must report only Canadian-source income pursuant to Part I of the Income Tax Act; treaty-resident status does not exempt business profits unless no permanent establishment exists (OECD Article 7 of the Canada treaty, typically Article 5 PE threshold at a fixed place or dependent agent; digital presence in Quebec without fixity may still create a deemed PE for online payment gateway operations).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 1, Lines 450–490 (Revenu Quebec CO-17, Box 180 and 185)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Deductions claimed including operating expenses, salaries, professional fees, transaction processing charges, chargebacks and reserve fund provisions, depreciation (capital cost allowance under Classes 50 and 52 for computer hardware/software), financing costs, and deduction of prior-year losses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident PSPs may only deduct expenses that are wholly attributable to the Canadian permanent establishment under section 4 and 115 of the Income Tax Act and must maintain revenue expense allocation records; head office general and administrative expenses allocable to the Quebec PE are deductible if properly supported by allocation studies and arm's length tests.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 7, Box 1–20 (Revenu Quebec CO-1108 and Schedule 12)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign tax credit computation, foreign accrual property income inclusions, foreign affiliate reporting, and transfer pricing adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident filing entity must report Canadian permanent establishment income and can claim an ordinary foreign tax credit for taxes paid to the residence country if the Canada treaty provides elimination of double taxation; TRC from the home revenue authority must be attached, and treaty re-determination under Article 7 prevents double inclusion.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 88 (Revenu Quebec CO-17, Box 400; Schedule 88)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax and minimum tax computation, provincial abatement, small business deduction, general tax reduction, and Quebec tax rate system including the 4% refundable tax on credit unions but not for corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporation's Canadian tax is calculated on net Canadian-source business income under Part I with no small business deduction unless the foreign corporation is incorporated in Canada; Quebec corporate tax rates for non-residents are applied to income allocated to a Quebec permanent establishment, and treaty benefits such as the M&P reduction may not be available without Canadian incorporation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 91 (Foreign Affiliate Information) and T2 Schedule 17, Line 700 (Revenu Quebec CO-17, Box 200)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Participation in foreign affiliates, controlled foreign affiliate (CFA) status, foreign accrual property income (FAPI), and transfer pricing documentation status under section 247 of the Income Tax Act.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident filing corporation that has a Canadian permanent establishment must disclose cross-border related party transactions involving the payment gateway's parent or subsidiaries, including merchant settlement flows, licensing fees, and intercompany management charges; TP documentation must be prepared within six months of filing the return and be available on request.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty under subsection 162(1) and 162(2) of the Income Tax Act is 5% of the unpaid tax when the return is late, plus 1% per full month for up to 12 months (maximum 17%), with an automatic increased penalty of 10% plus 2% per month to a maximum of 50% of unpaid tax where the corporation has assessed a failure to file in a prior period; Revenu Quebec imposes a similar penalty under section 1001.1 of the Taxation Act of 5% plus 1% monthly (maximum 17%), and 10% plus 2% monthly for repeat offenders (maximum 50%); both agencies apply interest at prescribed rates compounded daily (currently approximately 8%–9% for CRA and 8%–9% for Revenu Quebec) and can issue a demand to file or a deemed assessment under section 152(7) (CRA) and section 1084 (Revenu Quebec); a corporation that fails to file within the deadline may lose the Quebec deduction for late-filed loss carrybacks and must list the payment gateway's tax filings with both authorities; additionally, the CRA can impose a minimum penalty of CAD 100 for failure to provide information.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% for dividends paid or credited by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder under subsection 212(2) of the Income Tax Act; the rate is 25% for Quebec if the corporation is resident in Quebec and pays a dividend to a non-resident under the Taxation Act; the statutory rate is 25% but reduced under applicable tax treaties typically to 5% for a 10% shareholder and 15% for portfolio holdings when a treaty applies.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The Canadian payer or withholding agent must retain a completed Canada Revenue Agency Form NR301 (Declaration of Eligibility for Treaty Benefits) or Form NR302 and NR303 as applicable; non-resident beneficial owner must obtain a Certificate of Residence (or Tax Residency Certificate) from the residence country's competent authority and provide it to the withholding agent before the payment date; for Canada's treaty network qualifying for the 5% reduced rate on direct dividend holdings (e.g., Article 10 of the Canada–Luxembourg or Canada–US treaty), the non-resident shareholder must beneficially own at least 10% of the voting shares and be a resident of the treaty jurisdiction; the withholding agent may rely on the treaty declaration but must exercise due diligence and keep documentation for six years; for Quebec-qualified dividends, the province has no separate treaty withholding system but federal treaty relief automatically reduces the federal withholding portion and the provincial tax component is integrated with the federal 25% through the Canada–Quebec collection agreement; in practice, a cross-border PSP shareholder must file a CRA Form NR301 with the payer, obtain a TRC from the home country revenue authority, and if the payment is subject to Part XIII on remittance to a foreign parent, the payer must report using Form NR4 and file a NR4 Summary to the CRA; the audit risk includes the need to show beneficial entitlement, not a conduit arrangement, under GAAR and treaty anti-abuse rules.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rate for royalties under subsection 212(1)(d) and 212(1)(d.1) is 25% of gross royalty payments for the use of or right to use computer software, patents, know-how, trademarks, and other IP, reduced under the Canada–US treaty to 0% for software copyright payments or 10% for other industrial royalties depending on the royalty type; under the Canada–Luxembourg treaty royalty rates are 5% for copyright/industrial, commercial, or scientific equipment, and 10% for trademark/patent royalties; statutory interest withholding under subsection 212(1)(b) is also 25% on interest paid to non-residents unless the interest is arm's length in nature, in which case it may be exempt from Part XIII withholding if the payer and recipient are not related and the interest is on obligations listed in section 212(3) (e.g., arm's length debt obligations with a term of at least 5 years); under most treaties (e.g., Canada's DTA), interest withholding is reduced to 10% with the US under Article XI and to 10% with many other treaty partners, and interest paid to certain exempt pension or government institutions is 0% under treaty or domestic exception.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Mandatory contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation (Local File and Master File in the conventional sense) is not codified under a fixed CAD monetary threshold in Canada, but Canadian TP compliance under section 247 of the Income Tax Act requires documentation only when a penalty is sought; the CRA's administrative policy and evaluation thresholds set out that a penalty for a transfer pricing adjustment of CAD 10 million or more (subsection 247(3)) attracts a penalty equal to 10% of the adjustment if a document has not been prepared and provided within 90 days of a CRA demand; the CRA also requires that documentation be in place before filing the T2 return for transactions exceeding CAD 50,000 in gross revenue for each transaction class or where the value of the transaction is over CAD 1,000,000 in aggregate with a single related group, while the formal TP Master File/Local File documentation is recommended for multinational groups with gross revenue above CAD 50 million, and CRA Information Circular 87-2R clarifies the expectations; Revenu Quebec similar obligations are set out in section 1018.7 of the Taxation Act (the documentation requirements apply to corporations with gross revenue exceeding CAD 1,000,000 for each of the last two fiscal years and transactions with foreign non-arm's length parties exceeding CAD 1,000,000)
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP (comparative uncontrolled price) particularly for interchange fee benchmarks and merchant discount rates, Resale Price Method for payment gateway's reselling of acquiring services, Cost Plus Method for intercompany transaction processing fees and technical services, TNMM (Transactional Net Margin Method) for PSP subsidiaries performing routine acquiring and settlement functions, Profit Split Method for integrated global payment network services where both parties contribute unique intangibles such as proprietary fraud scoring algorithms and merchant relationships
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) as defined in the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Action 5 (BEPS) and implemented in Canada's GAAR (Section 245 of the Income Tax Act) and Quebec's anti-avoidance rule (Section 1099.1 of the Taxation Act) apply whenever an entity claims treaty or tax holiday benefits; a payment service provider operating through a Quebec subsidiary must demonstrate real physical presence, employees who conduct management and operational decisions in Quebec, full corporate records and bank accounts maintained at the Quebec office, and non-routine control of merchant settlement funds; a pure digital PSP that lacks a Quebec office and has only a registered agent will fail the economic substance test, be deemed to have a permanent establishment or sham, and attract recharacterization of revenue; the Quebec Business Corporations Act and Canada's corporate laws allow for a registered agent office, but the Income Tax Act's definition of permanent establishment requires a place of management or fixed base, thus a foreign PSP with a Quebec marketing office could be deemed to have PE; in addition, the Canada Revenue Agency considers the digital platform business to have a PE in Canada if it has a dependent agent who habitually exercises the authority to conclude contracts (section 253.1 and treaty Article 5); the ESR doctrine in Canada does not impose a fee-based regime as in the Cayman Islands, but economic substance is a factual requirement for treaty eligibility and for the payment of the 5% reduced withholding rate.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer pricing non-compliance and base erosion (Section 247 of the Income Tax Act)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A Quebec-incorporated PSP charges intercompany fees, royalty payments, management fees, or allocates profit offshore to a related non-resident payment processor at a price that deviates from arm's length rates, or fails to maintain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation for cross-border merchant acquiring and settlement service transactions; a particularly aggravated act is the "round trip" of license fees to a zero-tax jurisdiction for a risk engine or software that is actually developed in Quebec.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: A transfer pricing adjustment may be assessed against the Quebec PSP as if the transaction was at arm's length, with the additional taxable income subject to a 10% gross-up on the assessment under subsection 247(8); penalties under subsection 247(3) of 10% of the total adjustment apply where documents were not delivered within 90 days of a written demand, and interest accrues on the reassessment; a deduction denial on royalty payments may apply under section 18(1)(e) and 67.5 for unreasonable deductions, and a Part III tax under subsections 212(1) and 212(4) could impose 25% withholding tax on hidden distributions. Quebec may assess a provincial penalty under section 1029.9 of the Taxation Act of 10% of the Quebec adjustment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers of a PSP who participate in the creation of false transfer pricing records or who direct tax evasion are jointly and severally liable under section 160.1 and 160.2 for kiting and intercorporate transfers, and a court can lift the corporate veil under the Quebec Civil Code Article 317 where the corporation is a mere conduit; CRA can levy against personal assets and use collection procedures; a director may be personally liable for unpaid corporate tax withheld at source (subsection 227.1), and where fraudulent misrepresentation is proven, directors can face imprisonment under section 239(1) of the Income Tax Act (up to 5 years) and under section 992 of the Taxation Act (up to 5 years), plus penalties equal to 150% of the tax evaded.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax evasion and fraudulent misrepresentation (Criminal Code Section 380 and Income Tax Act Section 239)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully evading or attempting to evade Part I or Part XIII taxes on the cross-border payment gateway's income, including underreporting merchant acquiring revenue in Canada, hiding chargeback reserves, claiming fictitious transaction processing expenses, omitting Canadian-source merchant settlement fees, creating nominee shareholder structures to conceal beneficial ownership, or using false chargebacks to inflate deductible losses.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Summary conviction: CAD 10,000 fine and/or up to 2 years imprisonment; indictment: CAD 25,000 fine and/or imprisonment up to 5 years, plus court-ordered fine equal to up to double the tax evaded (subsections 239(1) and 239(2) of the Income Tax Act); Quebec Taxation Act imposes a penalty of 50% of the amount assessed where misrepresentation but not wilful default (subsection 1040), a penalty of 150% for wilful evasion and up to CAD 250,000 and/or imprisonment of up to five years for tax evasion (sections 996 and 997); the CRA will demand full payment of all taxes, interest, and penalties before the court hears an appeal, and a conviction triggers publication in the CRA's name-and-shame list (since 2014) of the individual and the corporation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly assent to or participate in tax evasion face personal criminal liability under subsection 239(1), and under Quebec under section 998 of the Taxation Act, and a director who is not individually named but whose acts lead to a corporate conviction may be charged with conspiracy or accessory liability; civil restitution is enforceable through a CRA Secured Certificate filed in Federal Court under section 223(2), which results in a legal hypothec on all property; directors can be prohibited from leaving Canada through a court order under the Criminal Code or the Income Tax Act, and a travel ban can be imposed upon charge; a director may also be disqualified from serving as a director under the Quebec Business Corporations Act and may be ordered to compensate the corporation or creditors of the sweep of funds.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Money laundering and unlicensed money services business (MSB) activity (Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), Criminal Code section 462.31)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The payment gateway transmits funds, clears merchant settlement, or provides payment processing services in Canada without holding a money services business license under the PCMLTFA (registration with FINTRAC as an MSB) and without maintaining a compliance program with a compliance officer, AML risk assessment, and transaction monitoring; aggravated act includes processing payments for a merchant involved in illicit goods and deliberately omitting suspicious transaction reports (STRs), failing to register the Quebec head office, or failing to maintain a transaction record trail, thereby creating a conduit for money laundering.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Unlicensed MSB activity can result in administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) under PCMLTFA up to CAD 3,000,000 per violation for corporate entities (Section 73.12), prosecution of senior officers under Section 74.1 for up to CAD 500,000 plus imprisonment of up to six months, and a court order compelling registration or shutdown of the business; failure to report suspicious transactions attracts AMPs of up to CAD 1,000,000, and laundering proceeds of crime under section 462.31 of the Criminal Code is indictable and punishable by imprisonment not exceeding 10 years; a designated business must have a compliance program that includes a written AML/ATF policies and procedures, training, compliance officer, and risk assessment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers of a PSP can be prosecuted under the Criminal Code if they direct, authorize, assist, or participate in money laundering, and the court may impose up to 10 years in prison; under the PCMLTFA, penalties may be imposed on individuals who agreed to the violation, and the director can be named personally; a conviction triggers a proscription of the offender from acting as director of any corporation subject to the Business Corporations Act for a maximum period of 10 years (federal Director's disqualification section), and civil asset forfeiture can reach personal property under provincial Quebec forfeiture rules (Section 7.1 of the Civil Code and Code of Penal Procedure provisions); a travel embargo is possible under the Criminal Code when a person is charged with money laundering involving foreign transportation of funds.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Ontario/Quebec licensing and unregistered payment processor (Quebec's Money Services Businesses Act and AMF/Ontario's Registration Act) – non-compliance with provincial payment processor licensing regulations
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating as a payment processor, merchant acquirer, or clearing house in Quebec without a license as a money services business under An Act respecting money services business (Quebec), being non-registered with Revenu Quebec for provincial sales tax (QST, TVQ) on merchant services, or failing to obtain the required authorization from the Superintendent of Financial Institutions or AMF for cross-border payment gateway activities; the act includes effective control of a PSP by a non-resident without prior approval for financial services M&A under the Bank Act and the Payment Clearing and Settlement Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: AMF may issue a cease-and-desist order and impose administrative penalties of up to CAD 500,000 for each contravention; Quebec legislation also imposes a maximum fine of CAD 100,000 for a corporation and imprisonment for affected officers in certain cases; failure to remit QST/TVQ on gateway fees attracts a civil penalty of 10% of the net tax amount and interest, and the Commissioner of Revenue may issue a corrigendum and impose fraud penalties of 50% or 150% if the omission is in bad faith; transactional money laundering under PCMLTFA may also lead to a federal injunction against the PSB, freezing all Quebec bank accounts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly authorize unlicensed activities are required to compensate any aggrieved merchant under Quebec's consumer protection and financial services legislation, and the Quebec enterprise registrar can cancel all permits if a director's individual licence has been revoked; Quebec courts may prohibit the director from managing any money services business; for a non-resident director, travel bans imposed under the Canada Evidence Act or provincial enforcement orders prevent re-entry into Canada until the statutory penalties are paid; and under the joint civil liability regime of the Quebec Civil Code Article 316, directors can be liable to the PSP's creditors when the business is operated contrary to public order.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to register as a resident corporation or permanent establishment and abuse of the limited liability vehicle (corporate veil piercing, misuse of agent agreements)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A non-resident cross-border payment gateway claims it is only a "agent" of the foreign parent, uses a Canadian "director nominee" to shield the true principal, and fails to file annual registrations, keeps no accounting records, transacts under the brand of a Canadian subsidiary without board meetings, or pays no corporate tax and allocates all profit to a foreign corporate treasury; a fatal aggravator is using a subsidiary ltd. that is not consolidated into any audited financial statement and never held an independent operational board.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA can treat the corporation as a sham or sham trust and assess tax on the true foreign parent under section 160, and can impose a penalty for false statements or omissions equal to the greater of CAD 100 and 50% of the understated tax (subsection 163(2), 20%; Quebec section 1040.1 at 50% or 150%); if the corporate entity is used to commit tax fraud or evade a liability, Quebec courts will impose civil liability directly on the sole shareholder and director under the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil; the name company's registration may be dissolved for failure to file the Quebec declaration immatriculation and federal annual return (Canada Business Corporations Act); unlawful corporate stripping of a Canadian active business results in the disallowance of the 50% provincial abatement and the application of the 25% withholding on deemed dividends to the foreign parent.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under subsection 227.1 of the Income Tax Act, directors are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's unremitted source deductions, and for unremitted QST and GST/HST (GST/HST section 323), and this liability can be collected against personal assets; Section 160 of the Income Tax Act may apply to transfer tax liability to the shareholder; Quebec allows a court order to seize personal property of a director who intentionally failed to observe corporate formalities; travel bans at the federal level are available under the Income Tax Act collection procedure when a director's debts exceed CAD 1,000,000 and there is a risk that the director will flee Canada; criminal liability can extend to a fine of 100% of the evaded tax plus imprisonment of up to five years; and Canadian immigration law (Immigration and Refugee Protection Act) excludes a director of a dissolved tax non-filer from entry where there are reasonable grounds to believe they are involved in organized criminal activity or misrepresentation for financial gain.
